subtopic: PROGRESS OF OPERATIONS IN SICILY-PARTICIPATION OF CANADIAN FORCES

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROGRESS OF OPERATIONS IN SICILY-PARTICIPATION OF CANADIAN FORCES
speechtext:
A week has now passed since the landing of Canadian troops in Sicily. I should like to make a brief statement on the progress of operations.
During the week, our thoughts have been mainly with the army. No account of the Canadian share in operations would be complete, however, without a reference to the other two services.
The battle for Sicily really began weeks before the landing of the allied troops on Saturday last. Ever since the close of the Tunisian campaign the allied air forces in North Africa and the middle east have been "softening up" the island of Sicily for the coming invasion. In those operations, Canadian airmen, in R.A.F. and in R.C.A.F. squadrons, have had1 a large share.
Operating under the immediate command of Major General James Doolittle of the United States Army Air Corps, an R.C.A.F. bomber wing composed of an unstated number of squadrons helped to pave the way for the allied invasion of Sicily by terrific bombardment of the island. During the landings and as the allied forces have continued to strengthen their position in Sicily, Canadians in the air have been blasting enemy troop concentrations, strong points and supply columns.
In addition to the bomber squadrons, a Royal Canadian Air Force Spitfire squadron which distinguished itself in the Tunisian campaign is participating in the Sicilian action. It cannot be revealed whether this squadron is yet based on a Sicilian field, but it is known that many members of the R.C.A.F. are among the aircrews which are now operating from captured aerodromes on the island.
There are, of course, thousands of Canadian personnel included in the Royal Air Force squadrons operating in the Mediterranean as there are in almost every R.A.F. unit around the world. No reports on their participation are available, but it is safe to assume that there are few, if any, Royal Air Force squadrons operating in the aerial forces being thrown against Sicily in support of our armies which do not include Royal Canadian Air Force personnel. Other Canadians are flying Wellington bombers, harassing and disrupting enemy supply routes from the African mainland.

The War-Sicily
While operations of our air units and our personnel out of the United Kingdom are not directly linked with the Sicilian campaign, their activities are having the effect of tying a great part of the Luftwaffe to Western Europe. Were these Luftwaffe units released for service in the Mediterranean they could make our operations there far more difficult.
In the Sicilian operations, the Royal Canadian Navy has also been represented. We have been advised that several hundred Royal Canadian Naval Officers and men acting in conjunction with and under the direction of the Royal Navy, took part in the hazardous work of safely effecting landings for the troops engaged.
For many months now, almost two thousand Canadian Naval personnel have been training at a combined operations base in England, * preparing themselves to take part in landing operations. Their ships are known as "assault landing craft". A number of Canadian sailors took part in the combined operations when landings were made in North Africa in November last. This week, they took their craft, under enemy fire, and ferried in troops who were part of the first wave of the invading forces to move on to the beaches. We shall await with interest a more detailed account of their hazardous work.
Coming now to the army, its operations began at dawn, Sicilian time, on Saturday, July 10, when the British, United States and Canadian troops commenced landing on the shores of Sicily. The landings on the beaches had been preceded by allied paratroop landings beyond the coastal defences.
According to statements made by prisoners, the landings were a complete surprise and caused much confusion. The element of surprise, combined with the fact that the landing areas were defended only by static or semi-static Italian troops, resulted in very light casualties for the landing forces. The bulk of enemy operational divisions were in the central part of the island.
The Canadian division, now identified as the first division, landed at the southeast tip of Sicily. Two and one-half hours after landing they had captured their first objective, and made contact with the British division on their right flank. Meanwhile British and American forces had landed to the east and west of the Canadians.
Canadian troops captured the airfield at Pachino six hours after landing, and a short time later were in Pachino itself.
On Monday, July 12, General Eisenhower visited the Canadians on Pachino peninsula. He sought out Canadian headquarters, but headquarters was moving forward so rapidly
that he was unable to make contact. That day the Canadians captured several inland towns. The first enemy counter attack was met and beaten off.
At Ragusa, an important inland junction about 25 miles northwest of Pachino, the Canadians made their first contact with the American forces.
I believe that this is the first occasion on which Canadian and American troops have been fighting side by side. We were, of course, both engaged in the last great war together, but I think this is the first time that Canadian and American troops have actually been fighting shoulder to shoulder in action overseas.
Shortly before midnight, Augusta, an important naval base, nineteen miles north of Syracuse was captured by British and Canadian troops. The port is stated to be in perfect working order.
On Tuesday, July 13, Canadian troops made further advances, repulsed counter-attacks and captured the first Italian general to surrender, together with his headquarters staff.
On Wednesday, July 14, Canadian armoured forces landed at Syracuse and moved north, while other Canadians were making progress over forty miles northwest of their landing places. It was revealed that day that the Canadians formed part of the eighth army, under the command of General Montgomery.
On Thursday, July 15, the eighth army including the units of the first Canadian division continued its advance along the east coast towards the Catania plains repulsing strong counter-attacks.
Yesterday, July 16, the advance continued on all sectors, and by the end of the day which completed the first week of operations, a wide arc enclosing about a quarter of the island had been occupied by the allied forces. Over 20,000 prisoners and a large quantity of arms and material had been taken.
So successful, within the week, has been the combined operations of the armed forces of the United States, Great Britain and Canada that yesterday morning, Mr. Churchill and Mr. Roosevelt felt justified in addressing to the people of Italy the proclamation which I read to the house at the opening of the morning sitting. The proclamation stated that the sole hope for Italy's survival lay in honourable capitulation, and that the time had come for the people of Italy to decide whether Italians would die for Mussolini and Hitler-or live for Italy and for civilization.
It is eminently fitting that the first division of the Canadian army should have been given the honour of taking part in the first major Canadian land operations of the war. The men of the first division were the earliest to volun-
The War-Sicily

teer; they have waited longest for action. They are the most seasoned formation of Canada's army overseas.
It will be a satisfaction to General McNaugh-ton, who led this first division when it sailed for Britain in the autumn of 1939, and who led parts of it to France in the summer of 1940, to have seen these officers and men, after three years of waiting, now carrying the fight into the enemy's camp with such conspicuous success.
Having this in mind, and realizing that the people of Canada would wish that an immediate word of congratulation should reach our troops upon their initial success, together with an assurance of our unfailing support of them, I sent the following message to General McNaughton on Monday last:
I know you must be exceedingly proud of the fine results of your long and ardous tour of duty. I congratulate you most sincerely on the achievement already evident in Sicily. Please arrange to have transmitted the following message to the Canadian Force Commander:
Message begins: Major-General Guy Simonds, Commanding Canadian Forces, Mediterranean.
"All Canada rejoices in the news of the initial successes of Canadian troops in Sicily. Will you please extend to the officers and men under your command every good wish for the complete success of the hazardous operations in which they are engaged. Here at home, in Canada, the eyes of all are fixed on Sicily. We know that there is heavy fighting ahead. We know, too, that the Canadian forces will do honour to themselves and to our country. Please give to all the assurance that our hearts are with them, that Canada is proud of the patience and courage of her army overseas, and that Canada will not fail her fighting men." Message ends.
We have reason to be thankful that the Sicilian landing operations were completed with very light casualties. Also that the resistance encountered during the first week of operations has ben comparatively slight. The successes of Canadian forces in the field should not, however, leave us unprepared for word of much heavier fighting which may follow at any time. There are strong enemy forces on the island and already stiff resistance has been encountered. Provided we guard against undue optimism, the people of Canada have every reason to rejoice at the results so far achieved in the first major operations in which the Canadian army has taken part. It is not too early to say that Canadian soldiers in Sicily are upholding the traditions established by the Canadian Corps of a quarter of a century ago.

Mr. Speaker, following the statement just made by the Prime Minister, I take it to read that the message to the Commander 
in Chief of the Canadian forces in Sicily was a message from the government and people of Canada to the forces under his command. I should like to ask the Prime Minister to couple it with a message from the parliament of Canada if that has not already been done in his message.
What the Prime Minister has said I think is most apt and appropriate in the circumstances. The upholding of the splendid traditions of our Canadian troops in these most recent operations is a matter of great national pride to Canada. While our troops have fought on many occasions with valour beside the troops of Britain and the other dominions, on this occasion our troops were fighting side by side with our American cousins to the south, and I think this will be hailed as another milestone in the close cooperation between these two members of the united nations who are engaged in this war.
We as members of the Progressive Conservative party want to join with the Prime Minister in the message which he has sent overseas and to ask him also to cable the good wishes and a good word from parliament itself.

subtopic: VISIT TO OTTAWA OF COMMANDING OFFICER OF FRENCH FORCES IN NORTH AFRICA

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: VISIT TO OTTAWA OF COMMANDING OFFICER OF FRENCH FORCES IN NORTH AFRICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is another matter or two which I think should be recorded in our Hansard
During the past week, as hon. members are aware, the government has had a visit from General Henri Giraud, the commanding officer of the French forces in North Africa, and copresident, with General Charles de Gaulle, of the French committee of national liberation. General Giraud is known to all for his heroism as a soldier, for his brilliance as a general, and for his complete devotion to the cause of France and of the united nations. He is the highest ranking representative of France to visit Canada since the black days of the summer of 1940. As a brave French officer, General Giraud is among the foremost of those who, throughout the war, have kept alive the military honour of France. In his own personality he embodies the heroic spirit of the French people.

Right Hon. H. V. Evatt
After his escape from Germany and German-controlled France, General Giraud's presence in North Africa, immediately prior to the allied landings, became a powerful factor in helping to rally all Frenchmen in Africa to the cause of the united nations. Without the liberation of North Africa, the invasion of Sicily, which has been so brilliantly commenced, could not have been undertaken.
General Giraud's visit enabled our government to receive at first hand a full account of developments in North Africa, and to discuss means whereby, in the coming months, Canada may be able to contribute aid to the French forces which now are taking their place with British, American and Canadian forces in the liberation of Europe.
Among the measures of cooperation which it is hoped to extend to the French national committee in Algiers is that of assisting, under our mutual aid legislation, in the training as aircrew, of a number of young French cadets from North Africa, in the schools in Canada of the commonwealth air training plan.
An especially pleasing feature of the visit of General Giraud to Canada's capital was the wholehearted way in which representatives of all groups of the supporters and friends of France joined in demonstrating the unity of their support for the French committee of national liberation of which General Giraud and General de Gaulle are the co-presidents.

subtopic: RIGHT HON. H. Y. EVATT   VISIT TO OTTAWA OP ATTORNEY GENERAL AND MINISTER OP EXTERNAL AFFAIRS FOR AUSTRALIA

speechtext:
Right Hon, W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):	Mr. Speaker during the
week, as hon. members are aware, the government has had a visit from the Right Hon. H. V. Evatt, Attorney General and Minister of External Affairs of the Commonwealth of Australia.
When Doctor Evatt last visited Ottawa, in the spring of 1942, Japanese threats to the security of Australia were very great indeed. During the months since, the combined efforts of the armed forces of Australia and the United States have held the Japanese enemy at bay and have frustrated his attempts to consolidate his hold on the land base which most nearly threatens the Australian mainland.
During his visit, Doctor Evatt discussed with my colleagues and myself possible means by which, under our mutual aid legislation, additional supplies might be made available by Canada to Australia. We also discussed means whereby assistance might be given in other ways which would serve to further the
common interests of Australia and Canada in the destruction of enemy power on the Pacific. Some aspects of post-war planning were also discussed. Doctor Evatt's visit served to emphasize how clearly the defence of Australia and the defence of Canada are both part of the world-wide fight for freedom. In particular, it helped to underline the extent to which the control of the northeast Pacific by American and Canadian forces, including the destruction of enemy forces in the Aleutians, is aiding in the final defence of Australia, just as the control being achieved by American and Australia forces in New Guinea, the Solomons, and elsewhere in the southwest Pacific, is aiding in the final defence of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege, which, I think, will be discovered to be a
Privilege-Mr. Hansell

privilege affecting every member of the house. I asked a series of questions some few days ago, which questions were passed as an order for return; it was in respect to the production and export of coal. The second question was:
What is the total tonnage of coal exported, and to what countries, for each of the years 1939 to 1943?
The answer comes, from the Department of Trade and Commerce I think, to this effect: In keeping with the present practice in the United States and the United Kingdom it is deemed inadvisable to state the importing countries. My point of privilege is that I am unable to get the information as to what countries this tonnage of coal vras exported to. May I now ask a question of the minister on the basis of the answer which I received here. Is the practice not to reveal countries to which we are exporting coal a temporary policy of the government on account of the war, or is this a permanent policy, that we are never to know what countries coal is exported to?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. HANSELL EXPORTS OF COAL-QUESTION AS TO DISCLOSURE OF DESTINATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can assure the hon. gentleman that the policy of the government not to reveal destinations of exports is purely a war matter. I may say at the same time that this matter gives us a very great deal of trouble. There are certain exports the destinations of which should not be revealed. I personally do not see much harm, if any, in letting anybody know to what country coal and certain other articles are exported, but it is hard to draw the line, and the practice generally followed is to maintain secrecy as to all exports.

speechtext:
The words "or subsequent" are added-"or subsequent to his conviction." I assume that some case has arisen which makes this necessary in the administration of justice. Perhaps the minister will explain.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It came about in this way. There was a tesd case before the court of appeal; the magistrate dealing with another case wished to have the benefit of the decision that would be given by the court of appeal before pronouncing sentence, and when the time arrived to recall the convicted person for sentence difficulties arose over this section in the code.

Section agreed to.
On section 7-"Common betting-place" defined.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO BETTING, PREVIOUS OFFENCE CHARGED, ETC.
speechtext:
The same principle is involved here as I was discussing last night in connection with another bill. It presses to an extreme degree the liability to prosecution by the use of language that is so conclusive and comprehensive as to take in almost anybody under any conditions whatever. The section as it stands now in the old act, giving the definition of a common betting-place, reads:
. . . opened, kept or used for the purpose of facilitating or encouraging or assisting in the making of bets upon any contingency or event, horse-race or other race, fight, game or sport, by announcing the betting upon or announcing

Criminal Code-Betting
or displaying the results of horse-races, or other races, fights, games or sports, or in any other manner. . . .
And so on. That is the present definition of a common betting place, and it is now sought to be amended by putting in the words "used or intended or likely to be" used for the purpose, and so on. That embodies the same vicious principle to which exception was taken last night. Section 8, the next section, applies the same principle to newspapers that circulate information calculated to assist people in betting, and now the mere fact of advertising the results of sports-baseball or any other sport of that sort-would render them liable to a heavy penalty. This is an indictable offence, making the accused liable to a year in gaol without apparently the option of a fine. "Used or intended or likely to be used." We know of places such as pool rooms and cigar stores where it is the custom for men to gather in the evening to learn, over the radio or otherwise, the results of sporting events of the day. It is now going to be made a penalty, a very serious offence, if you have a place where you do that, even if it is only "likely" to be used for that purpose-"intended or likely to be used." Is not that going rather far in restricting the liberties of the people? The explanation given on the opposite page is this:
The object of this amendment is to make more practicable the enforcement of the provisions of the criminal code with respect to betting.
I respectfully suggest that instead of making it more practicable it simply makes it easier and more convenient for the officers of the law. It is intended to make it easier for the officers of the law to secure conviction because at present they have to break into a place and find people engaged in betting and so on, and of course the material is there, whatever it may be. Now, however, it is simply sufficient to allege that the place is "intended or likely to be used" for the purposes mentioned. Surely that is carrying things too far. It is the old and evil doctrine of convicting a man first and letting him prove himself innocent if he can. Last night, speaking of a similar bill, the minister in charge, the Minister of Transport, was able to invoke the war as an excuse. It was a war measure, he pointed out, and we have to submit to certain restrictions of our liberty in war time, but that afterwards these restrictions would be removed. But this is not such a case, because we cannot conceive that the success of the war depends in any degree upon some petty cigar store being prosecuted for running a betting-place. And, as I say,
the penalty is severe. Such places are classed along with common bawdy houses as disorderly houses, and the penalty is up to one year's imprisonment and on repetition two years without a fine.
I suggested last night that in modern times the custom has been not to inflict very severe penalties with the idea of preventing crime. We have found that it is better, both from a humanitarian standpoint and as a matter of common sense, and moreover it is more effective, to make the punishment fit the crime without being excessive. Look back over history and you will recall that a hundred and fifty years ago it was' quite a common thing to deport people to Australia as criminals, and sometimes, going further back, to hang women for stealing a loaf of bread. Many instances are on record where such things were done. The idea behind such penalties was that extreme severity prevented crime. But the inhumanity of it dawned gradually upon people so that we no longer inflict such penalties.
I was curious to see what definition the dictionary would give of this word "intended," and I found it meant affianced lover. That did not give me much light. I want to know how anyone can tell what I "intend" to do under any given circumstances. I wonder the press gallery are not interested in this, because they also are liable under section 8.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: We have not reached section 8. If the hon. member will allow me to intervene at this stage I have an amendment to section 7 which will meet for the most part the objection he has voiced. Perhaps it would save time if I were allowed to put the amendment now. With respect to section 8 I shall have a modification to suggest which may facilitate discussion, but as regards section 7 I would move:
Strike out the second word "or" in line 35 and substitute therefor the following: "to be used or outfitted or equipped in such a manner as to be."
As amended it would read:
Used or intended to be used or outfitted or equipped in such a manner as to be likely to be used.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO BETTING, PREVIOUS OFFENCE CHARGED, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not
think that that carries the minister very far. It is a little more qualified, that is all; but the objection on principle remains. It is a question of intent. What is the equipment or outfitting that is had in mind? A telephone in a library or living room, or a radio might, in the opinion of the convicting magistrate, be sufficient to constitute a common betting-place. I do not know what gives
Criminal Code-Betting

rise to this particular class of legislation. I assume it arises out of the failure of the provincial authorities to get all the convictions they desire. It may be that they are justified in asking the consideration of parliament to this type of legislation. But I do suggest that it is a type which smacks of prohibition days, about which the hon. member for Essex East so often reminds me, and concerning which he expresses some surprise. While I do not think a high court judge would be influenced by this type of legislation to any very great extent, it is the sort of legislation which gives prosecutors and the type of magistrate we sometimes see on police court benches an opportunity to go much farther than they might otherwise go. That might be the effect, if the police magistrate had that particular type of mind which happens to be out on a witch hunt, where he would convict one of anything.
I should like to know the reason for this legislation. I remember in the days of prohibition having been shocked when I read of the sort of procedure, and the sections relating to prosecutions arising from temperance legislation of days gone by. In my early days as a lawyer I had a great deal to do with prosecuting, as well as defending, and most frequently came in contact with the old Canada Temperance Act. I was glad to lay down the burden when prohibition came in, because I did not want anything more to do with it. I suppose that in my lifetime I have been connected with at least five hundred cases having to do with violations of the liquor laws.

speechtext: That is, law cases.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO BETTING, PREVIOUS OFFENCE CHARGED, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, yes, not the other kind of cases. I was shocked to see the type of legislation these legislatures put into effect. It seemed to me that a good deal of it must have come from some of those fundamentalist states we read about, down in the south, where-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO BETTING, PREVIOUS OFFENCE CHARGED, ETC.
speechtext: Where they do not believe in evolution.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO BETTING, PREVIOUS OFFENCE CHARGED, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, where they do not believe in evolution, and where they frown on everything. In principle, this is the same kind of legislation; and unless the minister can show some real cause for it,
I do not think he ought to proceed with his amendment. I was surprised to find this provision in the bill, because from his statement upon introduction I understood there was to be in this measure no new substantive law. This is legislation of that kind, and I do 
suggest that it is a widening of the definition of a betting house or a gaming house, and that, therefore it changes the substantive law of the country.
Unless the minister can make out a case, I am opposed to this type of legislation. There is a burden of proof placed on the crown or upon the prosecution, and that should not be eased through the lifting of that burden by parliament, or by making it easy for a magistrate to elect that in the exercise of his judicial discretion he may place an interpretation upon a set of circumstances or a certain position which a reasonable man would not do. That, it seems to me, is the possibility under this amendment. The effect will be to make it easy to get convictions, in lieu of a position under which it was more difficult to do so. I hold no brief at all for betting, or anything of that sort. I do not take part in it.

speechtext: You should.

speechtext: Not this type of betting, bookmaking and the like. I do not think we ought to make it easier. I suggest further, that there is a principle involved. Before proceeding I say the minister must justify the use of this language.

Would the minister explain, when he rises to reply to the hon. member for York-Sunbury, what the amendment is going to be to section 8, so that we may discuss it now?

Provided however that the provisions of this paragraph shall not apply to the publication of news or records in relation to any race, fight, game or sport, or to contestants therein, in the ordinary course of publishing a bona fide newspaper.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO BETTING, PREVIOUS OFFENCE CHARGED, ETC.
speechtext:
That helps.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Before proceeding further may I make my position clear, because I believe what I shall say will be informative. The criminal law, including criminal procedure, is within the exclusive jurisdiction of parliament. But the administration of criminal law is within the jurisdiction and is the responsibility of the attorneys general of the provinces. It is perhaps the one instance in connection with which legislative jurisdiction is in one body and administrative jurisdiction is in one or more other bodies. This is the only place where an amendment can be made to the substantive law, or to the procedure. The attorneys general of the provinces have the responsibility of enforcing

Criminal Code-Betting
the law, and therefore they are closely connected with the application of the rules of procedure we lay down. From time to time they make representations to the federal department that, in their view, certain improvements should be made in the procedure. The stand taken by the federal department is that when a plausible case is made out for one of these representations it would be improper for the department not to bring it before parliament. Parliament is composed of people representative of the population of the whole country. They are at the same time inhabitants of Canada and of their own respective provinces.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO BETTING, PREVIOUS OFFENCE CHARGED, ETC.
speechtext:
The minister is carrying that doctrine further than his predecessor. He had to be convinced it was a proper change before he would bring it in.
Mr. ST. Then the amendment reads, "or outfitted or equipped in such a manner as to be likely to be used." The operation of a gaming house where people resort or have the opportunity to lay bets is a crime according to the law of the land. As I see it, all that is being asked for by this new amendment is that the crown be not required to prove something that it has been almost impossible to prove affirmatively, namely, that the premises have been kept or used for the purpose of facilitating bets.

Generally speaking, these particular provisions have been the statute law of the land for over forty years, or for almost one hundred years under the common law, without amendment. The modern bookmaker is able to evade the law as it stands at present. I feel that the objection which was pertinent when the bill was introduced, namely the words "or likely to be used" has been removed. As a matter of fact, I think the Minister of Justice is to be commended for having introduced the number of amendments he has. The criminal code is hopelessly out of date in many of its sections. There are a great number of anomalous sections and there has been no endeavour since our criminal law was first codified to revise it with a view to bringing it up to date. Different interpretations have been placed upon the same section by different courts. We continue year after year to use the same code, making only a few changes or adding a patch here and there instead of once and for all bringing it up to date after a period of fifty years. We should appoint a parliamentary committee, or a committee representative of the attorneys general and composed of outstanding counsel, to go over the code and bring it up to date, to the end that the purpose of the codification may be secured, namely, that the law shall be clear so that justice shall be done. Sections have been permitted to remain in the statutes which have no meaning whatever. "Or" has been interpreted as "and", an interpretation that is contrary to the actual intention. This is but one example of a section that should be revised.
I do feel that the minister should give consideration to the desirability of having carried out a piece of work that would be monumental in its results, that would be tremendous in its scope. It would require some years of effort, but it would make our criminal code something worthy of our country. Codification is intended to represent the law as it actually is at the moment it is codified. I ask the minister to give consideration to taking what I believe would be one of the most forward-looking and advanced steps that could possibly be made, namely, the removing of the anomalies that now exist in many sections and the recodifying of the criminal law thereby bringing it up to date and in accordance writh modern practice.

speechtext:
In my opinion the amendment proposed to be made by section 7 to section 227 of the criminal code is most objectionable, and I think the amendment which the Minister of Justice moved this morning, if I understood it correctly, is almost equally objectionable. This amendment is a departure from one of the fundamental principles of our criminal law-that before a person can be charged with a crime he must have committed an overt act or must have failed to do something which the law says he shall do. This amendment makes it a crime for a person to have a wrongful intent. It is a retrograde step, an encroachment on the principles of British justice. If this amendment becomes law it places in jeopardy the freedom and security of the citizens of this country. It seems to me that if there is one duty more than another that members of parliament owe to their constituents, it is to be zealous in guarding their freedom and security and maintaining the fundamental principles of British justice.
In the fourteenth century the opinion was held by some legal authorities in England that the intention to commit a crime constituted an offence. In the sixteenth century such an objectionable doctrine was overruled, and the principle was established that the intention to commit a wrong was not in itself a crime. The reason for this change in the law, I think, is obvious. It was made, I believe, because of the extreme difficulty, if not impossibility, of proving what was going on in another person's mind at a particular time, and because of the fact that even if that were proved, it was impossible to find that that person might not on further consideration change his mind and commit no offence. This amendment, if it becomes law, is a step back towards the middle ages.
In Holdsworth's History of English Law, volume 8, page 443, I read the following:
It was well settled in the 16th century (in spite of the opinion to the contrary held in the 14th century) that a mere intention to commit a crime, unaccompanied by any overt act, entailed no criminal liability. "The imagination of the mind to do wrong" it was held in Hales v. Petit (1563) Plowden, page 259, without an act done, is not punishable in our law, neither is the resolution to do that wrong, which he does not, punishable but the doing of the act is the only point which the law regards; for until the act is done it cannot be an offence to the world, and when the act is done it is punishable.
That case quoted by Holdsworth was decided in the reign of Queen Elizabeth.
I turn now to a judgment delivered in the twentieth century, to a judgment of Mr. Justice Riddell, of the Supreme Court of

Criminal Code-Betting
Ontario, in the case of Rex v. McCarthy, decided a few years ago, and I read these words:
. . . an intent is not enough for as Chief Justice Bryan said in Year Book 17 Edward IY, 2 pi. 2-
I might say that this case was decided before the reign of Queen Elizabeth:
"The devil himself cannot try the thought of a man".
And Judge Riddell adds:
It would he hopeless to look for greater subtility in the courts. Intending to commit a crime is not the same as attempting to commit it.
Our criminal code provides that a person is liable to a year's imprisonment who is found guilty of keeping any disorderly house; that is to say any bawdy house, common gaming house, or common betting house. A common betting house is defined by section 227, which is the section now proposed to be amended, as:
A house, a room or place (d) opened, kept or used for the purpose of facilitating or encouraging or assisting in the making of bets,
And so forth. That is a good definition. That is a real definition of what a common betting house should be. But this amendment would change that definition. It would define a common betting house as a house, office, room or place used-and here are the words to which I wish to call attention-"or intended, or likely to be used, for that purpose". The definition goes altogether too far; it makes an intention a crime.
I would ask hon. members what they would think if a person in their constituency was summoned to court charged that between a certain day and a certain day in a certain month he did unlawfully intend to keep a disorderly house, to wit, a common betting house at a certain named place for the purpose of betting contrary to section 229 of the Criminal Code of Canada. A man is charged with the intention of doing something, charged with an idea he has in his mind and which he may subsequently change. The whole thing is absolutely wrong and is absolutely out of place in this age.
What a man may intend to do and what he actually does are, very often, two entirely different things. Second thoughts are often best, yet under this amendment it is an offence to intend to do an act even though that intention is not carried out and the act is never done. It seems to me that this is going entirely too far, and that you cannot justify upon any principle a law of this kind.
There are various classes of crimes. Some are more serious than others. Betting is not
one of our more serious crimes; in fact some corporations are permitted under certain statutes, restricted as to time and place, to operate pari-mutuel systems of betting. Why should it be necessary to make such a drastic alteration, for a minor crime, in the principles of our criminal law? It seems to me that that is a question which is hard to answer. A precedent should not be established. We are told, in the explanatory notes to this bill, page 2, that under the code as at present worded-
. . . the crown, in order to obtain a conviction, must prove that the house, office, room or place alleged to be a common betting house was actually opened, kept or used for the purpose ... of facilitating or encouraging or assisting in the making of bets. . . .
I submit that that is exactly what should be proved if justice is to prevail in this country. A man is presumed to be innocent until he is proved guilty, and it seems to me that the onus should be on the crown to prove that the house, room or place alleged to be a common betting house was in fact used for that purpose by the accused, before it can obtain a conviction for the offence.

I wish to add just a
word as to the principle of criminal law which I am sure interests everyone who has had anything to do with the administration of justice in this country. I must confess that I agree with those who oppose the introduction of the principle of finding a person guilty on the basis of an intention, or on the basis that a certain thing is likely to occur. I do so for two reasons, one of which has been touched upon already by the hon. member for St John-Albert. The safest principle for criminal law, which is a penal statute, is to have an overt act a necessary ingredient of the crime. We all recognize that almost every human being has his moments of anger, his moments of ill-advised passion, and that often, mentally at least, he contemplates what would be a crime, serious or otherwise. In the great majority of cases, thank heaven, that intention is never carried into effect, and no overt act is committed. If we attempted in our criminal code to punish every person who intended or had thought of doing a criminal act, it would be merely a farcical attempt to enforce an impossible law.
I agree with other speakers; I know of no habit that will so surely sap the strength of a nation as widespread gambling, yet it seems to be inherent in human nature to wish to gamble in one way or another. There is, therefore, a certain similarity between this evil and that of bootlegging, let us say; and from the experience we gained in attempting to control the liquor traffic we know that in the last analysis all law must have a measure of public support. If you do not have that support your law will not be efficacious in its application. I suggest to

That a select committee be appointed to examine the expenditure defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for the defence services, and for other services directly connected with the war, and to report what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government may be effected therein, and that notwithstanding standing order 65 the committee shall consist of twenty-four members, as follows: Messrs. Black (Cumberland), Blackmore, Boucher, Pinard, Cleaver, Coldwell, Donnelly, Dupuis, Fauteux, Ferland, Gladstone, Golding, Graham, Homuth, Hurtubise, Jackman, Hill, Nixon, O'Neill, Picard, Pottier, Reid, Sissons, Winkler, with power to send tor persons, papers and records; to examine witnesses and to report from time to time to the house.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the terms of reference of this motion are similar to those of the motions in two previous years for the appointment of the war expenditures committee, the only difference being in the personnel of the proposed membership. Along with other members of the house I regret that the committee has not been set up earlier, but hon. members who follow the proceedings will, I am sure, appreciate the reasons for that. At an earlier stage in the session I indicated that I was most anxious to have all the standing and select committees set up at as early a day as possible. Indeed, such a request was made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon), and the government sought to meet it. I believe the standing committees were appointed earlier this year than they have been at any other session for years past, and the same is true I believe with respect also to the special committees. But it did happen that on the motion for the appointment of one or two special committees there were long debates, and as the government had before the house financial matters respecting the war which it was recognized were all-important, it was thought inadvisable to present this particular motion at a time when it was likely to hinder the progress of the government's financial measures. The most important measures, as members will recall, were the mutual aid bill, the war appropriation bill and the budget. The budget, which was brought in at a very early stage of the session, occupied time that would otherwise have been taken for the appointment of this among other committees.
I wish to draw the attention of hon. members to the statement which I made in the house on April 10 and, which will be found in
Hansard at page 2290
Another matter which was stressed at the beginning of the session was that the government should appoint the committees at an early stage. of the committees in readiness and sought every opportunity to have them appointed at an early date. But there is still on the order paper, as hon. members are aware, notices for twp committees, one with respect to war expenditures and the other with respect to radio broadcasting. I think I did mention at an earlier stage of the session that we took about a week in appointing the committee on social security and the committee on reconstruction and rehabilitation. Those committees might have been appointed in five or ten minutes and we could have had the discussion at a later stage. The main purpose is to get the committees appointed.
If it is at all possible I should like to get the committee with respect to broadcasting and the committee on war expenditures appointed before we adjourn for Easter. speechtext:
Now that almost four years have elapsed since the beginning of hostilities, and about nine billion dollars have been spent in the prosecution of the war, it is obvious, I think, that some check on war expenditures on behalf of the members of the House of Commons is important. It is difficult to reconcile the importance of the war expenditures committee with the fact that the session has run from January 26 until the present time without this committee having been set up; indeed, that with such colossal expenditure going on the committee has not been in deliberation since about the middle of last November.
The composition of the war expenditures committee, consisting as it has done of twenty-four members, eighteen of whom are appointed from the government side of the house, and six from the opposition, shows that the opposition members have very little control over the workings of the committee. This is the third year of operation of the war expenditures committee, and so far no opportunity has been given members of this house to discuss the matters which the committee should investigate or the recommendations they have made. This is the sort of opportunity that is afforded us, in the dying days of the session, on a Saturday afternoon, when a great many members have already gone home. Add to that the fact that this war expenditures committee, from its inception, has been sitting in camera and that the individual members of the committee are in honour bound to observe secrecy, to make their inquiries without the help of expert evidence, without technical assistance, to get what information they require as best they can, and on information so obtained to base their recommendations, having little or no opportunity to carry out any real research before submitting their findings to the membership of the House of Commons. So far as I am concerned, that is not just democracy. It is not representative government, and it does not represent to the members of the House of Commons the true functions of the war expenditures committee.



War Expenditures Committee
There are no doubt occasions when secrecy and sittings in camera are necessary. The war expenditures committee could and perhaps should deal with many matters that carry with them possibilities of giving aid or comfort to the enemy, and in that event no publicity should be made possible so that information may go to sources that should not have it. I fully appreciate that. But I well recall, as a member of a subcommittee last year, a motion being brought before the committee to discuss war-time housing in public, and that motion was defeated-despite the denial of the member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver)-and the committee went into the subject of war-time housing.

Under the circumstances it did not seem to me, as an individual, that I could properly discharge the functions of a member of a political party, a member of His Majesty's Loyal Opposition-the official opposition-a member of the House of Commons of Canada and one who, representing a constituency in this house, has a duty to perform to his country beyond his constituency, beyond his party, beyond the official opposition. For when committees meet in camera, one must keep one's information to oneself. Every member of such a committee must observe the conditions of secrecy, and therefore cannot be given a proper chance to discuss or explain matters in the house.
Let me discuss, as I see them, the advantages or otherwise of sitting in camera. There is no doubt that when you sit in camera certain information can be given to the committee, which would not otherwise be obtained, with regard to matters on which the enemy should not be informed. But there are other aspects as well. We all know that, even when

meetings are held in camera, witnesses come before the committee in almost every instance with a brief prepared either by themselves or b3- the departments they represent or by companies or corporations for whom they are working. Such briefs are prepared with the minutest care, and on many occasions they were read to the committee. On a few occasions briefs were left with the committee for discussion and evidence was taken from them. Not only were briefs prepared in advance, before witnesses came before the committee, but on many occasions the Department of Munitions and Supply, and sometimes solicitors representing a company, were there with a watching brief to see that nothing was said that should not be said. There was therefore ample safeguard against undesirable material coming before the committee, without the necessity of sitting in camera.
In my particular subcommittee, as I believe in others, when secret information was given we were warned, and I believe the members of my subcommittee were particularly cautious not to disclose anything of a secret nature. On this point, I suggest that any gentleman is unworthy of membership in the House of Commons if he cannot use his own discretion to observe secrecy where necessary. Many committees sitting in camera can on occasion hear evidence that should not be repeated to the public, evidence that should be withheld from the press and kept off the record. But let me point out that when the witnesses give evidence before the subcommittee it is taken down by shorthand reporters and a copy is given to the witness. They have every privilege of changing it or of deleting from it anything they consider should not be in it. They can check' it or modify it. But one thing I did' observe and did resent was the fact that the members of the subcommittee sitting in camera could not obtain for their own use a transcript of the evidence taken from day to day. To be sure, they could go to the branch and look it over and leave it there, and sometimes they could take it out and bring it back; but in my opinion, doing the work that I felt called upon to do, as I am sure every member of the subcommittee on which I served also felt bound to do, through long periods of the holiday last year, and going through evidence of all sorts, the members of the subcommittee should have a transcript from day to day of the evidence taken so that they might peruse it carefully and make comparisons. They would then be in a better position to verify their reports, because they would be more conversant with all the material that had been submitted. But

War Expenditures Committee
in analysing the evidence that was given my powers were very limited. Indeed, I was very much impressed by the extent to which that limitation went, and many times I felt how futile it was for me to give an opinion and back up that opinion with any assurance without having expert or technical assistance to that end.
Let us take for instance a production plant [DOT]-Toronto Shipbuilding, let us say, or the Noorduyn aviation plant, or any plant you wish. We look over their payrolls and see that they have 9,000 or 10,000 men, with salaries ranging all the way from high brackets to low brackets. These workers are producing intricate mechanisms costing hundreds of thousands of dollars. How can we analyse the financial set-up of a company of that kind, without the assistance of someone versed in financial matters? How can we go into their books to find out if their excess profits taxes are correctly paid, what profits they are making, whether their costs are proper and economical, or whether their subcontracts are efficiently handled? For members of a subcommittee to go to a war production plant, in which colossal production is being carried on, a committee asked to produce an analysis without the assistance of expert evidence or expert help, is just like glossing over the surface. It is like putting wax on an already veneered surface.
Before we continue we should look into that phase of the matter. I do not cast any reflection upon the honour or the integrity of any witness coming before the committee. I have no reason to do that; but it has been argued to me that if the committee, sits in camera a witness can give evidence which is open and frank and complete. As a practising lawyer I have always felt that the best test and assurance of veracity and exactness is a sworn oath given in public. The whole set-up of our courts in Canada is based upon public hearings, and it has been done in that way for the protection not only of the witnesses but of the public. In my view the test of publicity is a most advantageous factor in any discussion of this kind. We know that our courts decline to accept evidence given on affidavit, because they realize that in respect of those affidavits there is no opportunity for cross-examination. The rules of evidence applying in our courts have been framed after years of experience in trying to get the best possible evidence. A person giving evidence before a subcommittee on war expenditures should be sworn. That person's evidence should be transcribed as sworn. Then it should be given to the members of the committee for their deliberation, and it
72537-315*
should be given the test of publicity, so far as it can be given. It should be given to the scrutiny of persons specially skilled in analysis of cost accounting, to a chartered accountant, or to some expert of the kind.
The subcommittee on which I have served has on a number of occasions called in people who were specially skilled in respect of certain work, and have asked them for their point of view in inspect of problems brought before us. That itself is illustrative of the necessity of having expert technical assistants before these subcommittees. If one were to look over last, year's report of the subcommittees and to investigate closely the ground they touched upon and the work with which they were charged, he would realize at once that thirty subcommittees, let alone three, could not properly discharge their duties. I repeat that before the committee on war expenditures can make a thorough investigation and report its findings with certainty and with assurance -and it should be in that position before it reports to the house-it should have at its disposal every possible facility for going into all the minute details with the utmost thoroughness. Here we are setting up, during a recess, a committee of twenty-four members. Undoubtedly it will be subdivided into three subcommittees. One of the subcommittees will be asked no doubt, to deal with government corporations, shipbuilding and aircraft production. To ask a subcommittee to handle that amount of work is to ask it to do not the work of a. few days, not the work of a few hours a day, but the work of years.
It is my frank opinion there is no limit to the amount of work the committee on war expenditures could do. There is grave danger in asking a subcommittee to deal with subjects much too involved and too intricate for their consideration, unless they have expert assistance. Some time ago the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) stated in the house that the war expenditures committee was investigating contracts. Well, if any hon. members present to-day remember the big books of contracts we had placed before us- books laden down with contracts-they will realize at once how utterly impossible it would be for any subcommittee even to scratch the surface of investigating such contracts. And the fact that between November 13 and this date the committee has not sat cannot help but reflect an opinion held by the government either that there is a lack of necessity for the setting up of the committee, or that the committee could not do its work well.
As we enter the fifth year of the war we should take some of these facts into consid-

War Expenditures Committee

eration. I believe that at least some advantage can be gained by a subcommittee on war expenditures sitting in camera, even though its findings cannot be passed on. As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has said, the very fact that the committee on war expenditures is sitting may do some good. But that is not good enough for the people of Canada, and it should not be good enough for the 245 members of the House of Commons. A committee on war expenditures, if it is to be adjudged worthy of its existence at all, is worthy of serious consideration, serious discussion, and the serious analysis of hon. members of the House of Commons.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been a member of the committee on war expenditures since it was first established. As such I recognize I have a considerable responsibility to the house and to the country. Parliament has been most generous in voting money, and the people of Canada have supported its parliament in those expenditures. In fact in their desire to have the greatest possible effort made in .the carrying on of the war, our people are ahead of the government. It is the responsibility of parliament, one which has been passed on to a committee composed of representatives in parliament, to see that these moneys are properly expended.
I was not anxious to serve on the committee on war expenditures. In fact I can say I was adverse to serving on it. I was not able to attend at all times. I had responsibilities to discharge to my constituency, to my home and to my business, with the result that I was unable to attend at all times when the committee sat. I feel that .there must be some greater appreciation than obtains at present as to the immensity of the work devolving upon this committee. If the committee is to discharge its duties properly it should have been sitting continuously.
The hon. member who preceded me said that billions upon billions of dollars have been voted for war expenditures. In the fiscal year 1942-43 the vote for war expenditures amounted to three and a half billion dollars. When we reassembled in January we had to provide for a deficit of $858,000,000, nearly a billion dollars. Surely that is a great responsibility to be placed upon the committee charged with examining expenditures, to see that they are properly made. This parliament for the fiscal year 1943-44 is voting five billions of dollars for war expenditures and another $500,000,000 for civil expenditure. And if the experience in other years is repeated we will be faced with another deficit in this fiscal year. This means

an expenditure of $15,000,000 a day. To a great extent the public will hold this committee responsible for the proper expenditure of these tremendous sums of money. I want to say to you, Mr. Speaker, that as a member of that committee I must admit that I have not fully discharged that responsibility, and I can make the further admission that as a member of parliament I do not think I am capable of dis-iharging that responsibility to this parliament and the people of Canada as it should be discharged.
There has been a great deal of adverse criticism of expenditures. The people are willing and prepared to have us vote all the money necessary and put the entire credit of this country at stake; but there is a great deal of misgiving in the province of Nova Scotia and all over this country that this money has not been always properly expended, and that there has been waste and extravagance. I have heard that said a hundred, a thousand times. The country was full of rumours of extravagance and waste at the time the construction work was going on at Debert, and we have not checked up on that. There were rumours of extravagance and waste in connection with Deep Brook at Windsor and the eastern passage airport. It was suggested that this latter work should have been investigated by our committee, but a special commission was set up, consisting of the late Hon. W. N. Tilley, K.C., who investigated the project and made a report. Nothing has been done with respect to that report, either by the war expenditures committee or by parliament, though it contained a very damaging finding to the effect that the successful contractor had obtained inside advance information. Apparently he was allowed an arbitrary advance classification of materials in connection with the eastern passage airport, which the other contractors were not given. The explanation was that he had asked the government officials and they had given him this arbitrary classification, which I think was ninety per cent earth and boulders, six per cent earth and four per cent solid rock. He also figured on a much greater yardage than the other contractors, expecting that additional yardage would be removed. That was unfair to the other contractors; that was not a proper standard to set for contracts involving the expenditure of millions of dollars; yet nothing has been done about it.
If we are to have a committee of this kind it should be in continuous session. No evidence has been taken by this committee since last November, though it is true that the committee sat for a few days prior to the opening

War Expenditures Committee
of this session in January, to draw up a report, and it is also true that the committee came to a unanimous conclusion. None of us on that committee is looking for scandals; certainly I am not, but we have a duty to see to it that the money is properly expended and that sound policies are laid down by the government. We have a duty to safeguard this country against waste and extravagance, but we have not been able to perform that duty; we have not done it, nor are we now capable of doing it. If we were to undertake to discharge that duty we would have to sit continuously, and not have an interval of eight months with no sittings at all, while expenditures are being made at the rate $15,000,000 a day, with an over-expenditure or deficit of $858,000,000 last year and a war appropriation this year of $5,000,000,000, with probably another overexpenditure or deficit of a billion dollars coming, to judge by the experience in the past.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that I do not believe the members of this committee are capable of performing the duties expected of them by the people. I have nothing but good-will toward the other members of the committee. Our relations during the sittings of the committee have been exceedingly friendly, and I believe we have given each other our complete confidence. But the public expect more of the opposition members than they expect of supporters of the government. On one occasion this session the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) took the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) to task for not having fulfilled his duty in this regard as leader of the opposition. I believe the public hold us responsible to a greater extent than they do members of the government party to see that these public moneys are properly expended. There are only four members of the official opposition on this committee with three subcommittees-four out of twenty-four on the committee. The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) made an appeal, I think to this house but certainly to the committee, for a larger representation from the opposition. It is true that we have a representative of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party. It is true we had last year a representative of the Social Credit party, the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston), with whom we worked in close accord. The responsibility placed upon those six representatives of the opposition parties, if you want to style us all in that way, is an impossible obligation which I, as one member of parliament, with my responsibility to parliament, to my electors and to the people of this country, have not been able fully to discharge no matter how greatly I desired to do so.
I have nothing but goodwill for the other members of this committee, but many of them have obligations to the government. As our first chairman we had a very capable member, but I think I am fair in saying that his primary duty was to see that the interests of the government were protected. I refer to the former hon. member for Selkirk, now Mr. Justice Thorson, who became a member of the government. His successor was the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Fournier), the present Minister of Public Works, his primary and immediate duty also was to see that the government's interests were protected, that we brought in a proper report reflecting credit upon the government at all times. We also had as members of this committee hon. members who have since become parliamentary assistants, and others who are looking for favours from the government.
It is my opinion, Mr. Speaker, that this committee, as it has been set up, cannot investigate these enormous expenditures and safeguard the public interest as the public expect it to do. Now the question arises whether at this late date, under existing circumstances, it is proper that we should once more assume this responsibility, whether in doing so we can do justice to ourselves, to parliament and to the people of Canada. In view of the information I have; in view of what has taken place; in view of the decision of the committee to sit in camera on matters such as war-time expenditures for housing, and so on, I have grave misgivings as to whether I should continue as a member of this committee. I owe some duty to my constituents, to my family and to myself. More is exacted of those of us who come from the far east and the far west, in discharging our duties here, than is required of members from central Canada. I have been away from home practically continuously for six months, and I do not know that very much more should be expected of me. I gave the assurance to my electors, as I have given it to parliament, that I would make any personal sacrifice in order to discharge my duties and contribute in every way possible to the winning of this war, and I am prepared to stand, by that undertaking, but I am doubtful about serving on this committee further.

As a member of the war expenditures committee I wish to say a word or two on the resolution, in view of some of the remarks that have been made. Considering the importance of the committee I think that certain information should be given to other members of the house who are not members of the war expenditures committee, because the question has been asked by members of the House of Commons, how did we employ our time; and there was a feeling that we were not utilizing all our time as members of the committee.
Subcommittee No. 1, of which I had the honour to be a member, studied all agreements and put on record a synopsis of them. They had every company making aeroplanes appear before the committee and the fullest opportunity was given every member to ask questions. We visited every aircraft plant and took a record of the financial set-up, going into the matter of profits and capitalization and looking over the balance sheets as best we could. We investigated salaries and high wages. We investigated hours of work and wages paid and made recommendations accordingly, because we did find in some instances that salaries had been greatly increased. We checked up on all these matters and reported on conditions generally. We found out how the employees did their work, the hours of labour, employment of women, cafeterias and restaurants, and whether the call-up by the draft board was affecting production. These are some of the things done by members of that subcommittee. The work was most interesting.
With reference to the expenditures that Canada has made on the war the question has been asked how a small committee such as has been set up could ever begin to look into all these outlays that have taken place. I would compare what we are doing with what has been taking place in Great Britain. In Great Britain they are spending an average of $60,000,000 a day and have a total committee of thirty-two members. Our expenditures will be between $14,000,000 and $15,000,000 a day and we have a total of twenty-four members; so that we are not very far out of line. As a matter of fact, if the argument advanced to-day is sound, Great Britain has not nearly sufficient members on the committee there; yet there has been no complaint from Great Britain regarding the wTork of that committee. I would have liked to see, and would still like to see, the members who go on that committee adopt the attitude of members of the British House of Commons. It was stated, and one will find it in British
War Expenditures Committee

Hansard, that the select committee over there felt that they were the trustees of the House of Commons as well as of the country, not the trustees of any party. They were not only the trustees of a constituency, but the trustees of the entire country. And when I acted as a member of the committee-I believe those who were members will support what I am going to say-I did my utmost on behalf of the people of this country, not on behalf of a constituency alone or a party, to find out what those companies were doing.
I am somewhat annoyed to hear members of the committee complain that there are not enough Conservatives on the committee or not enough Cooperative Commonwealth Federation members on it. I think we should be adopting an attitude such as was adopted in the British House of Commons-and it is to be seen in Hansard-where when they joined the committee they left their politics behind them, and represented the whole country. They did not represent any party or constituency.
We have heard some talk this afternoon about secrecy. Well, I have been long enough in the House of Commons to realize what has taken place and what does take place in committee meetings, so that I am in a position to compare open meetings with those held in secret. While I find no fault with the press at all, I do remember one committee which sat this session, which I think illustrated the point I am going to make. At the time I have in mind, during the present session, two committees were sitting on one day. One of those committees was deliberating on social security, but not a single press reporter was present. The committee was alone. The press reporters were to be found in the committee which was endeavouring to find out where the rugs were located. While I could not see one press reporter in the committee where they were discussing the welfare of our people, there were sixteen in the other committee. One could hardly get in where they were investigating Colonel John Thompson, and finding out who had got a rug or an armchair. I say then that if we had held our meetings openly, apart from the inadvisability of doing so, I doubt if we would have conducted any business at all. And I say without fear of successful contradiction that if we had held open meetings we would have had press reporters there, and members rushing in with prepared speeches stating that they had heard so-and-so, or rumours here and rumours there. To my mind the business was conducted splendidly in camera. If every member would go to that committee, with the
[Mr. Reid.)
idea in mind, not of party but of the House of Commons and the people, there would be no need to complain about any lack of representation.
The committee in Great Britain did not even report to the Prime Minister of Great Britain or to the cabinet ministers. They were not allowed to do so.

A great deal has been accomplished, and we can take pride in what has been accomplished since the report was laid before the house in January. Hundreds of thousands of dollars have been saved through the deliberations of that committee. ,1 believe that the committee should deal with all accounts, and that the committee should be empowered to go into the affairs of concerns engaged in war work, with respect to their set-up and their balance sheets.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make one or two observations before the motion carries. In the first place I have been at a loss to understand the Prime Minister's reason for not having set up the committee before. I recall that from the very first he said this committee would be set up as soon as the war appropriation bill was passed. That was the main reason for not having set it up. Well, he did go ahead and set up a lot of committees of much lesser importance than this one.
Those of us who sat on the war expenditures committee-and I can speak with greater authority for subcommittee No. 1, because that was the one on which I served-were almost unanimously of the opinion that the committee Should sit continuously. If it was to do beneficial work, it should sit not only when the house was in session, but when the house was adjourned; it should sit all the time. I am in agreement with hon. members who have said there is a tremendous amount of work to be done. Unless the committee is sitting continuously it cannot perform its duties in the proper fashion.
As to the work of the committee last year, I believe that after all our work we had just reached the point where we could thoroughly perform our duties. We had just got to the place where we knew what to look for when we went into a plant; we had just reached a point somewhere near efficiency, when the meetings of the committee were suspended. That was most unfortunate. The excuse or reasons the Prime Minister has given for not setting up the committee are at least ill founded.
There is one other thing I think should happen, if this committee is to perform its duties properly. I agree with the hon. member for New Westminster when he says that periodical reports should be made to the house. I believe the work of the committee is of such importance that members of the House of Commons generally should know something about what is going on. In that connection it should be possible in some way- I do not know just how it would be done-[DOT] to inform members of the committee as to what action the government has taken or intends to take as a result of recommendations made by the committee. I feel quite certain that when the committee made recommendations last year the government acted upon them immediately. The committee, however, was not informed of that action. As a member of the committee I do not know that the government acted upon one solitary recommendation. Surely that is a wrong procedure.
Members of the committee would receive a great deal of encouragement if they knew their recommendations to the government were receiving serious consideration. Whether such report from the government should be made to the house or to the committee would be a matter for the government to decide. But certainly there should be some means of knowing what action was being taken.
It is true that the work of that committee is very important. I was one who thought it should sit continuously, and while it sat I pressed for that very thing, along with other hon. members. I do not wish to leave the impression that I was the only one. I wish to commend the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) for his statement that he at least viewed the work of that committee in a non-partisan way. I believe he did, and I believe other members did, also. I believe that was the attitude of most of the members of the subcommittee on which I was working, and of course I became better acquainted with them than with the members of the other subcommittees, because we were in daily contact. Generally speaking the members of that subcommittee, including the chairman, performed their duties not from any political point of view but with the desire to see what they could accomplish.
That brings me to the question of the representation on the committee. I made this objection when the committee was set up a year ago; I repeated it when the committee had its first meeting, and I make it again to-day. I do not think the representation of the members of the house on that committee is fair and proper, though in this my view is probably contrary to that of the hon. member for New Westminster. Take the Social Credit party, for instance; we had one representative out of twenty-four. You may say that was fair in proportion to our membership in the house, but let me point out how it was unfair. The main committee was divided into three subcommittees, each of which had its own work to perform. We went for days without seeing the members of the other subcommittees at all; we might be away on the other side of Canada when subcommittees one or two were sitting, and in fact that very thing did occur. One of the other subcommittees brought in a report, which was accepted unanimously, though the member's of the other subcommittees knew nothing about it. That is the position in which I was placed, as a member of the Social Credit party. There was the report of a subcommittee, of which I knew nothing at all but to which I was expected to give my consent; and apparently I did give my consent, because the report was adopted. That should not be the
War Expenditures Committee

case; certainly I should not be asked to give my consent or approval to something of which I had no knowledge. Therefore I am going to repeat the suggestion that I have made several times previously. If the main committee is to be divided into three subcommittees, there should be at least three members on the committee from each party in the house; three from the Social Credit party, three from the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, and three or six or whatever is considered to be fair from the Conservative party. I do not think I can be accused of being politically-minded in making that suggestion; I make it purely from the point of view of fairness to the different parties in the house.
Then there is another matter to which I should like to draw your attention, Mr. Speaker; that is, the way the business of the committee is conducted. I am not so particular whether the meetings are held openly or in camera; I can see some advantages in holding them openly, and I can also see advantages in holding them in camera. There is no doubt that sometimes more information can be obtained when the meeting is held in camera. The Gimli affair has been referred to. I do not think there was anything in connection with that matter which could not have been brought out in an open meeting, and probably our work would have been more effective, but on the other hand there are times-
