I am trying to suggest improvements for the next committee, and I think that is an essential improvement. When this government is put to the expense of bringing witnesses all the way across this country, or, on the other hand, of sending the committee across the country, the evidence that is given should be absolutely correct; there should be no misunderstanding about it, and witnesses should be held responsible for the evidence they give. I am not going to refer to the instances I have in mind, but they were outstanding, and this is one of the matters that should be dealt with first by the new committee.

War Expenditures Committee
There is another change that I think should be carried out by the new committee; that is,
I do not believe the legal adviser of the Department of Munitions and Supply should be sticking around all the time. He was the biggest nuisance we ever ran across. Personally he was a fine fellow, but he was always there, trying to protect the department. As a matter of fact in some cases the witnesses were so confused that they would not give their evidence, and that is not a good thing. The new committee will find that unless they rectify that situation and keep this gentleman away, they will not get the evidence they should get. I remember that on one occasion we had to ask him to either get out or shut up, he was becoming such a nuisance, but that is not the important thing. The important thing is that when you have legal representatives there it throws a psychological atmosphere around the witness which you do not want present.
There is another thing-I seem to be finding a lot of fault with this committee-which I believe is quite important. Hon. members will recall that when this committee was being set up a year ago I stood in the place in which I am standing now and asked that a proper secretariat be appointed. I think the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) supported it. But we did not get any support in the house. When we went into the committee we again asked for it, but we did not get it. But when the committee had finished its sittings last year, I believe I am correct in saying that the members were almost unanimous in their approval of the appointment of a proper secretariat for the committee.
It is an overwhelming job for the ordinary layman to investigate these tremendous amounts and the way in which they are spent. Few members of the committee were capable of properly analysing an audit sheet or of saying whether the audit sheet brought before the committee was the one shown to the directors of the company. I am informed that that was not the case in many instances, that the audit sheets shown to the committee were not the audit sheets shown to the directors of the company. Only a legal man or a chartered accountant would be able to discover that. Every precaution should be taken to see that the information brought before the committee is authentic and that the committee is given the opportunity to delve as deeply as possible into these matters. I do not believe that can be done unless the committee has at its disposal a proper secretariat. Last year we found ourselves handicapped on many occasions because of the lack of that service. It is unfortunate that such a secretariat has not been set up long ago.
Another objection which was raised last year when the committee was first set up was that it was exceedingly difficult for members to be here all the time. After sitting continuously in the house for six or seven months, hon. members found it exceedingly difficult to sit here another three or four months. I was here last year for nine and a half months, and that is a long time to be away from home. You have to let your other work go. Members from the west had to stay here; they could not get home for week-ends as some hon. members can when the house is sitting.
There is no reason why this committee should not have been set up the first week the house opened. I think every member of the committee last year was in agreement that it should be set up just as quickly as possible so that they could perform the duty assigned to them. I am not a member of the committee this year, but I wish to express the satisfaction I had in working on the committee. I found that the members were conscientious and endeavoured to investigate these expenditures to the best of their ability. They did good work, and they saved the government a large amount of money. The exact amount I do not know, because the government has nearer reported back to indicate that it has acted on the recommendations. It would greatly encourage the members of the committee if they knew that the work they were doing was appreciated and had been acted upon.

Mr. Speaker, before this motion carries I should like to make one or two observations about this motion standing in the name of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). We are now in the one hundred and thirteenth day of this session of parliament. In other words, almost six months have expired since the house first convened for this session. This motion of the Prime Minister to set up a committee to examine the expenditures defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for the defence services has been standing on the order paper of the House of Commons since February 24.
I have just made reference to the orders of the day of. Friday, February 26, and under government notices of motions I find four motions for the setting up of committees. The first appears in the name of the Prime Minister and had to do with a committee on social security; this first appeared on February
War Expenditures Committee

16. The next motion, which appeared on February 19 in the name of the Minister of National War Services (Mr. LaFleche), was for the setting up of a committee on radio broadcasting. The third, which appeared on February 19 in the name of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Michaud), had to do with the committee on Canadian National Railways. The last one appeared on February 24 in the name of the Prime Minister, and has now been reached on July 17.
It is well known that the progamme of legislation is in the hands of the government. If this committee is essential now in the view of the government, it must have been essential in February of this session. It was fourth on the order paper to which I have made reference, and it has been the fourth or last to be called. But the government had it in its power to have altered that sequence, and this allegedly most important of the committees which were to be set up could have been called before any of the others. That was a matter which lay entirely in the hands of the government and the government must take the responsibility for it.
Mention has been made in previous debates -not in connection with this motion because there has been no debate on it-by the Prime Minister to the delays which have occurred, partly owing to the fact that amendments had been offered to the motion to go into supply. I do not suggest that the Prime Minister was blaming the official opposition for this; in fact I know that that was not in his mind, but I am bound to say that the official opposition has not moved an amendment to the motion to go into supply during this session. I think that ought to go on the record, because if there is blame attachable to any group for delaying important legislation, it should be attached where it properly belongs.
It is interesting to note the delays which occurred in connection with the setting up, prior to the Easter recess, of the reconstruction committee and the committee on social security. I checked Hansard and, speaking of delays, I found that in the reconstruction committee debate, 65J columns of Hansard were used by government meipbers, 42J columns by the official opposition, 31J columns by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, and 49J columns by the Social Credit group. I am not finding special fault with that; but since mention had been made in a previous debate of delays that were said to be attributable to other parties than the government and perhaps to ourselves as the official opposition, I thought the Prime Minister and the government would like to 
have the record straight. A similar situation existed in the debate on the social security committee. I have not the figures before me, but I am safe in saying that a similar situation existed there. I hesitate to raise this question and would not have done so, had it not been that some mention was made of delays on a previous occasion.
The Prime Minister to-day in launching his motion made quite a proper reference to certain financial matters of importance which perhaps should have the right of way over some other matters that the house might wish to discuss, including the setting up of committees. I think no one in the house would have any quarrel with the Prime Minister with respect to the importance of the financial measures because, after all, it depends very largely on the situation in which one finds oneself and the programme of the house. But prior to the budget debate there were debates on the setting up of the reconstruction committee, the social security committee, the radio broadcasting committee, and now we are debating the setting up of the war expenditures committee. I can recall that there was some lapse of time between the beginning of the debate setting up the reconstruction committee and the social security committee and the commencement of the budget debate.
I think the house generally was of the opinion that the budget and certain other legislation had to come before this house and be passed before March 31. I quite understood, and I think members of the house generally understood that there were provisions in the budget which made it essential that it should be brought before the house and passed before that date. But, as it subsequently turned out, there was no such necessity. As a matter of fact the legislation which was supposed to be so essential was not passed by that date. In that connection may I point out, Mr. Speaker, that if we had taken an extra half-day or even a Saturday, because one Saturday is as good as another for doing the country's business, or if we had given up a Wednesday evening or a Friday evening, these matters which some members regarded as important could have been disposed of earlier. So that the Prime Minister's argument that the war expenditures committee could not be set up earlier because it would interrupt or delay the passing of the war appropriation measure falls to the ground. Even to-day we have set aside the war appropriation measure, which we said previously we could not do, in order to discuss this very motion. It seems to me there is not very much difference between

War Expenditures Committee
intervening on July 17 and intervening some time in May or March or April in the debate on the war appropriation measure or the budget.
We have now lost ninety-three sitting days so far as the setting up of the committee on war expenditures is concerned. If the government consider that this committee is doing the kind of job it ought to be doing, it seems to me that those ninety-three days were precious, and if they were precious, the committee should have been set up. If they were not precious, there is no particular reason why the committee should be set up now, in the last moments of the dying days of a dying session. Whether by design or by accident, the fact that the government have not attempted to set up this committee before is a tacit recognition on their part of the weaknesses of the committee itself.
What opportunity will there be to deal with the report of the committee that is being set up now? We shall be into another session before there is an opportunity to deal with the report of this session, and surely we are not gong to be put in the position of having to deal with the report of a previous session as well as the report of the current session.
But there are other reasons which I think I ought to bring before the government why the motion should not have been presented at as late a date as this. It has been mentioned by other members of the house, and I shall not repeat at any length their arguments. A distinct and important advantage would have resulted if parliament had taken advantage of the ninety-three days we have been sitting here, during which members could have conveniently served on the war expenditures committee because, if the committee is to sit between the adjournment of this session and the beginning of another, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston), not only is it inconvenient to bring twenty-five members of the house to Ottawa to sit on the committee during the recess, but there is also the question of the expense, and expense to-day is an important matter. The expense of carrying this committee during the recess will be very much greater than if it were sitting during the session. That is an additional reason why I think the government will have to accept a heavy responsibility for not having brought this motion before the house sooner.
There is another angle with *which I should like to deal. I have never had the privilege and responsibility of serving on the war expenditures committee, and perhaps may deal
with it in a more detached way than those who are close to the work. The views I express could perhaps be taken as the views of those who look upon the committee as the public would do.
One of the features of the operations of this committee in the past which has aroused public dislike-and I say this very kindly to the committee and the government-is that it has abused its privileges, particularly in having recklessly gone into secret session much too frequently. I realize that the Prime Minister and other hon. members will have their own answers on this point, and I am quite willing to maintain an open mind with respect to it. But in dealing with expenditures, whether for war or any other purpose, supreme care should be taken lest people get the idea that you are trying to cover up something when you are trying to find out what is wrong. I have never yet been able to comprehend why the majority membership of a committee allow subcommittees to sit in camera on such a wide variety of subjects.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: I gave the hon. member one reason.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I know. I am not going to argue with the hon. member at the moment. But as regards the holding of secret sessions, why was there any necessity to deal, for example, with wartime housing in a secret session? How is the national security menaced as far as wartime housing is concerned? That is only one subject which might be brought up.
After all, hon. members have a sense of responsibility with relation to national security in time of war. Hot one of us would willingly allow a single bit of information to go from him or from any committee on which he sat, or from this house, which would give one iota of aid or comfort to the enemy. But with respect to matters which might almost be termed peace-time activities, such as the housing investigation, I believe the action of the committee in sitting in camera has done more than anything, else to bring its operations into disrepute. I am not making any charge, but here is what people will say: a committee entrusted with the investigation of the expenditure of public funds, of money which is actually collected in the open, are pursuing their inquiries behind closed doors. The public do not want the committee to be just a plaything of the government; they expect it to be a watchdog of the people's interest. That is something which we as members of parliament must carefully bear in mind.
A few moments ago the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver), in interrupting the
War Expenditures Committee

hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) made what I thought was a significant statement. I was suspicious of the situation and I think his remark would convince almost anyone on the point. Surely we have not arrived at the position so far as these committees are concerned that in order to have unanimity in a report we must sit in camera. Let us not have unanimity in reports of committees if in order to obtain it we must pull down the blinds and close the shutters on the committee's structure.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit an interruption?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Does not the fact that a unanimous report is reached suggest to the hon. gentleman's mind that the correct solution of a contentious problem has been found?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I would say that as far as the government is concerned a solution of a contentious problem has been found, but as far as the people are concerned it may be an entirely different matter.
The same principle seems to me to apply in connection with other subjects. Take the debate with respect to the wartime information board, whose expenditures relative to publicity were before this house not long ago. Hon. members will recall at once the answer returned by the government to the two motions which we made, in order to get before the public accounts committee the matter of the expenditures of the departments on publicity. "We do not want to send it to the public accounts committee," the government said in effect, "we want to send this to the war expenditures committee." How are you going to have an investigation of the wartime information board if you allow the setting-up of the committee to be delayed until the end of the session? That surely is not an argument worth speaking about. Further than that, was there any reason why the wartime information board's activities should not be open to public scrutiny? Was there anything to the argument that national security is in any way affected? I do not think any hon. member would go so far as that. After the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) had made an impassioned speech in this connection in defence of the government, and had said in effect, although not in so many words, that perhaps it was not advisable that the investigation should be held in open in the public accounts committee, I asked the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar), who was temporarily leading the house, "Will you undertake that, if the matter goes before

the war expenditures committee, that committee will not sit in secret with reference to the wartime information board?" And he said, "I will give you no such undertaking." Technically, perhaps, that may have been right, but in every other respect, viewing the moral aspect of the matter, it was wrong. So that we find that the wartime information board, instead of being investigated by the public accounts committee, was shifted to the war expenditures committee, which has not been set .up until now. I need not point out in any further detail the difficulties and the delays involved in this proceeding.
I know the sort of answer which will be made from time to time as regards public sessions of committees. I realize as well as the Prime Minister or anyone else the frailty of human nature. But in all seriousness I point out that, with the public gaze directed upon expenditures generally, while perhaps here and there a subject may arise which the government would feel should be dealt with in camera, there are thousands of places as to which the bringing of the facts into the light of day will not only have a beneficial effect on the particular transaction, but it will do more. If every department of government recognizes that it may at any time be drawn into a wide-open investigation, with the blinds up and the doors open to the public, that will have as salutary an effect on departments generally as anything I can at present conceive; because the very threat of having the light of day shed upon any department of government makes for good government and discourages the opposite. That governments and parliaments are constituted as they are, with the checks and balances of government and opposition, with oppositions being given in peace time at any rate, and to some extent in war time too, a measure of freedom to criticize, subject to the national inteVests generally, is the reason why democracy has functioned as well as it has. The people realize then that their representatives can open up and turn the searchlight on wrongdoing, and it is a good thing for the government, because in every action they take behind closed doors of the cabinet council there is always in the back of their minds that they must come into the chamber and defend the expenditures they have made and stand up for the policies which they have put into effect. That is why democracy has functioned as well as it has. But the very moment people get the idea that there is such a thing as closed doors, even though it may be argued that there is no harm in going on, as will no doubt be argued by this government, they will say that where-

War Expenditures Committee
ever there are investigations to be made, they must be made in such a way that the public of Canada shall know what is going on and what the remedies are.
Here is the hon. member for flow River this afternoon- making a speech in which there is evidence of a good deal of knowledge with reference to this matter, which of course he could not disclose, and going so far as to indicate that although his subcommittee had made certain recommendations for a better policy in certain departments, he had not even heard whether the government had entertained any of the recommendations submitted or made use of the information and advice given. These are matters, too, which we must consider in connection with a motion such as this.
The object of publicity is to prevent wrongdoing. Let me make my position quite clear. I do not want to be raising scandals against this government in war time. I may as well tell the government that. Every move that I have made as leader of the opposition or as a private member has had regard to that principle. I have not made a single move, so far as I am aware, that has had behind it the intention of raising scandal. More than that, I have no use for those whose only object is to go on a fishing expedition or a scandal-mongering expedition or to try to do something of this kind in order perhaps to weaken the government's position in war time. I have no use for that type of public or private citizen at a time like this. We cannot afford, in a serious war-time period, to have enemies in Canada. -Our enemies are not Canadians; they are in Japan, Italy and Germany. I often think that we should re-orient our position in regard to our petty differences so as to recognize the importance of this point. It should be recognized by people in public life generally. That is important. But as regards just and honest criticism of the expenditure of public moneys, criticism that is made not for the sake of going on a fishing expedition or a scandal-mongering expedition, we should be sensible, because it is the people's money that is -being spent, not the government's money or our money. Keeping that in mind, we should let the people know what is being done. Surely that is not too much to ask of the goverment and -of -this parliament at this particular time.
A. relentless scrutiny of public expenditures is essential to proper war-time administration, and it is more essential from the point of view of the government -than from that of any -other section of the whole dominion, because the responsibility rests upon them.
I was very much impressed by some of the arguments brought forward this afternoon by
those who have had some experience on committees such as this, who felt their helplessness and their inability to study in detail the various contracts that had been entered into and the expenditures made. We are spending money at the rate of eleven times as much as we did in 1936 when the budget was brought down. We can realize, therefore, with the vastly swollen expenditures to-day, the result of the war, with all the ramifications of government business, that even the government itself must find it very difficult to keep abreast of developments. And yet twenty-five members of parliament are trying to investigate these expenditures, hardly any of them having any really technical knowledge of the various subjects into which they are inquiring. No matter how capable they may be in their several ways; no matter how conscientious, surely it is not necessary for me to tell the members of this house just how far the committee can make a detailed investigation and give a report which would be really intelligent, having regard to the tremendous volume of business in which the country is now engaged. The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) admitted his helplessness, and I am sure the members of the committee generally are conscious of their incompetence for want of technical assistance. As the hon. member for Cumberland and others have pointed out, there is not the proper technical help; there is not a proper secretariat, which would bring to these various matters the kind of advice that is so essential if the work is to be carried on as it should be.
I think that ought to be fairly well recognized by everyone in the committee; and that, I suggest, is one of the weaknesses of the committee. The committee has to open the door and let in the light of day. Sittings in camera have become the rule rather than the exception, and that is the reason for the abuses against which I so strongly and vehemently protest this afternoon.
I wish to say this, that I am unable to support the motion of the Prime Minister; and the reason why I am not going to support the motion of the Prime Minister with respect to the setting up of this committee revolves around the necessity, I think, of some party in this house rising up and taking some decided, definite and effective stand as a protest against the secrecy of the sessions of this committee on war expenditures. In addition to that, I do so in order that we may also effectively protest against the lack of adequate representation of our party on that committee. Another effective protest, or reason for protest, lies in the failure to set up the committee at a previous time in the session. The Prime Minister himself must
War Expenditures Committee

recognize that most, if not all, of his reasons for setting up the committee are all gone, because we are now in the last week of a long session, and the committee has not yet been constituted. We take this position, too, as a protest against the lack of proper technical organization in the committee, and proper organization so far as the question of secretariat and experts to assist the members of the committee is concerned. That, it seems to me, too, must be protested against. We felt that the most effective means by which we can protest against these abuses, and against these irregularities which are going to reduce materially the effectiveness of the committee, would be to oppose the motion which has been made.
And more than that, I wish to say clearly that if the government proposes to go on, and the committee is set up, we must reserve our rights, as members of the Progressive Conservative party, with respect to making a decision to sit on those committees, particularly where they are being held in secret, and dealing with questions where actual national security in our opinion is not involved. In this way I place before members of the house our position. I do so because I feel that after all, great as were the aims and ideals of this war expenditures committee, the abuses which have crept in and the situations which have arisen from time to time have placed our party in the position where we have felt that some effective protest in the national interest is essential at this particular time.
Therefore, at this time, in closing my remarks, I desire to say that for the reasons which have been advanced we shall oppose the motion of the Prime Minister.
Mr. T. J. O'NEILL (Kamloops): Mr. Speaker, I have listened this afternoon with a great deal of interest to what has been said from the floor of the house with respect to this war expenditures committee. I have listened to the reasons why the committee was not set up sooner, as expressed by some hon. members, and reasons why it possibly should not be set up at all.
This afternoon the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) has made a strong appeal against the setting up of this committee. He is a man for whom I have the greatest respect and regard. As a matter of fact, so much do I regard him that I say this now, without fear of successful contradiction, that unless Mr. Bracken gets a seat for himself in this house very soon there will not be any necessity for him to be here at all. That is the kind of a job I think the leader of the opposition is doing.

There were several objections he made which were not clear to me. First of all, he regrets exceedingly that the committee was not set up. Then, in his last words, just before he took his seat, he tells us that he opposes the setting up of the committee. That is the opinion that was going around this house just before Easter, namely, that if the government attempted to set up the committee the opposition would oppose it.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Who said that?
Mr. O'NEILL: The hon. member asks who said it. I am telling him that that was the popular rumour in the house. That is who said it. But now the leader of the opposition tells the house he is going to oppose the setting up of the committee. It does appear that there must have been some foundation for the rumour going around the house. So that it does seem to me the government cannot be blamed very much because of the failure to set up the committee, when the opposition were going to oppose its being set up.
Just now reference was made to a unanimous report being brought in by the committee. The leader of the opposition has said that, so far as the government is concerned, yes; but so far as the public is concerned- well, that is another matter. I was not a member of the committee last year, but I was the year before, and I resent that remark a little bit. It seemed to me that he sort of cast a reflection upon those members of the committee who were from the government side.
Then the leader of the opposition complained about the percentage of representation of his party on the committee. So far as I am concerned I cannot see that there is any difference between the percentage of representation of Progressive Conservative members on that committee and the percentage on other committees. There is no different attitude taken toward the Progressive Conservatives from that taken toward any of the other parties. It is all based on percentage. It may be urged that that percentage is wrong. But my belief is that it follows the representation throughout the country. For instance, Ontario has a certain number of members in the House of Commons, and it is based-or is supposed to be-on a percentage of population. The same applies in setting up committees of the house. The Progressive Conservative party has twice as many representatives as the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation or the Social Credit party, because of the number of members in the official opposition party in the house.
Then some hon. members-and among them, I believe, the leader of the opposition-have

War Expenditures Committee
complained about lack of control in the committee. It does not seem to me, Mr. Speaker, that any party should have control of a committee, and I do not think there was any attempt to have control. Certainly on the committee on which I served no attempt was made to have control of the committee. So far as I am concerned, in all the committee meetings I attended there were only one or two occasions when in my opinion it would have been quite all right to hold the meeting in public; or at least I could see no very good reason at the time for its being held in camera. But there was this point to be considered at all times, that we would get far better information, and get it more readily from the witnesses, if they were assured, before giving their evidence, that the meeting would be held in camera.
It was our idea to get that information. We were not trying to uncover any scandal, because we believed that the people in this country were just as sincere in their war effort as we were. Therefore there should not be any scandal to uncover, and we were not trying to uncover any. What we were trying to find out -was if there was any way whereby we could improve methods employed in doing their business. One particular instance I have in mind had to do with the head of one of the large hospitals in Canada, a man who did not have to come before the committee at all. Quite definitely that man would never have appeared before the committee, unless the meeting had been in camera. The things that he might say might be misconstrued by some member of the press. He was not in there to give information, unless it was on the understanding that the meeting would be in camera. I did not see any reason in the world why we should not hold that meeting in camera. Certainly no information was going to develop which would be of comfort to the enemy, but that was not the point. We wanted to get information, and the only way in which we could get it was to guarantee to that gentleman that the meeting would be held in camera. That was done; we secured the information, and I think some good came of it.
Some hon. members, including the leader of the opposition, have complained because the government brought in a motion like this on a Saturday afternoon, when everyone had gone home. I ask, why have they gone home, with the house still in session; why are they not here? That is what we have to contend with all the time with these "T-to-T" members -Tuesday to Thursday; those of us who come from the maritimes or from the west are here from the middle of January until the
middle of August, while these other hon. members slip out on Thursday and do not come back until the following Tuesday. Now they have the audacity to complain in this house because something is brought up on a Saturday afternoon and they are not here. Well, they should be here. I maintain that it is absolutely wrong to blame the government for bringing in this motion at this time. I may be a little dumb, but I do not see how the government could have done anything else, because on the very statement of the leader of the opposition it would seem that this matter would be opposed no matter when it was brought in.
Something has been said about publicity. In my constituency I have not heard one person, whether he belonged to the Liberal party, the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party or the Progressive Conservative party, say anything that would lead me to believe he was suspicious that this committee was trying to cover up something. I never heard any such suggestion. Publicity, you know, at times is very much abused by all political parties, and sometimes it seems to me that we make too much use of it. I was at a League of Nations' meeting not very long ago at which one speaker said the public men of this country were destroying the confidence of the people in them. That speaker was a university professor, and he said one of the things that was undermining the confidence of the young men and young women of this country in our government was that the Progressive Conservative party had made too good a job of tearing down the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). That is the kind of stuff that is going on in the country; that is the sort of thing that is making the people believe there is something wrong in our government institutions. I have not seen anything of a crooked nature since I have been here. There are many things about the government of the country that seem wrong to me, but I have seen nothing absolutely crooked1. Yet there is a great deal of talk in this house, coming from all political parties, trying to make out that there is something wrong with those who belong to the opposing parties.
There is not very much else I wish to say in connection with this motion. I was not on the war expenditures committee last year, though I was on it the year before last and I saw nothing wrong at that time. So far as I am aware no graft was proved, and I have no knowledge of what was done in connection
War Expenditures Committee

with the report last year, whether or not it was acted upon. However, I am sorry that this committee was not set up long ago, for there is no doubt that people are going to wonder why that was not done, and why the committee must sit while the house is not in session. Personally I feel that there is so much business for that committee to attend to that it should sit all year, whether or not the house is in session, and we should not have to wait until the house meets again, to have the committee reconstituted. It should go right to work and keep on working, and even then it would not be able to look after all the business.
There is another complaint that is often made, in connection with the attendance of hon. members in this house, which I think might be answered at this time. We have had five or six special committees,' in addition to the regular committees of the house, and very often when you come into this chamber you find only from twenty-five to forty members in their places. I have had visitors sitting in the galleries who have asked me where all the members are. Well, the members are attending these various committees, and I suggest that if this committee had been set up as well, with twenty-four or twenty-five members, wre would have had a hard time to get a quorum There is a limit to the number of committees that can be set up with only 245 members, and there is a limit to the efficient work that can be done by those committees. Personally I am very sorry the committee was not set up sooner, but certainly I am going to support the motion, and I would suggest to the Prime Minister that, if it can be arranged in any way, the committee be set up again as soon as we meet next session, or that the present committee be continued, so that it may go right on with its work.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say to the members who have served on war expenditures committees how deepfy the government appreciates the services they have rendered in connection 'with the committee's work. I was reserving what I wished to say on that point until the conclusion of the debate. I believe there are very few tasks more important or more onerous than the task which is assigned to hon. members who sit on the war expenditures committee, particularly when that committee is obliged to hold its meetings not only while parliament is in session but practically throughout the year. As some hon. members

have mentioned this afternoon, this means a very great sacrifice not only of time but of personal means and in relation to their own business affairs. I believe this service merits the thanks of all members of the House of Commons. In the name of the government I should like to express very sincere thanks to the members of the committee for the efficient and helpful service they have rendered.
I am at a loss to understand the attitude of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) in saying that he does not propose to support this motion, for the reason, as alleged by him, that he wishes to make a protest in the matter on behalf of his party. Well, in listening to him, I thought he was protesting a good deal. If that is the real purpose behind my hon. friend's decision not to support the motion, I should certainly feel that purpose had been adequately served by what he has said. However, I would point out to the leader of the opposition that he like myself is a salaried officer of this house. He has his duties as leader of the opposition and I have my duties as Prime Minister. One of his duties as leader of the opposition is to see that the house is informed at any and all times when there is reason to believe that the government is not doing its duty. I ask hon. members to look through the proceedings of parliament of this session and see if they can find at any time in any place where the leader of the opposition asked that the committee on war expenditures should be immediately appointed. He may have done so in some general statement with respect to the calling of committees generally, but he has seen this motion on the order paper; he has heard it called from time to time, and never once has he risen in his place to say that it was in the public interest that the war expenditures committee should be appointed, that its setting up should not be delayed and that he would ask the government to set apart a time when the committee could be set up. I say that if he had done that there might have been some reason to believe that his intention not to support the setting up of the committee was based upon the reason that the government had not done its full duty in the matter.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group, did not rise in his seat to express the hope that the committee would soon be establshed. The reason I gave him at the time for its not having been established was that an agreement had been reached between the leaders of the different parties in this house that certain other business would be proceeded with first. As leader of

War Expenditures Committee
this house I feel myself to be bound by agreements reached in matters of procedure of business of the house as in all else between the different leaders in the house. As hon. members know, there was a distinct understanding between the leaders that the financial measures would be disposed of as rapidly as possible and that the order of procedure would be as set forth in the agreement which had been reached between us.
If I had been asked to waive that agreement; if I had been told that there were special reasons why it was desirable that it should be waived, I would have been the first to have met the request. I was anxious to get the committee appointed. I made that perfectly clear in statements which were made when the house was about to adjourn for Easter. I said that I was very anxious to get the remaining two committees established before we adjourned, the one on radio broadcasting and the other on war-time expenditures. The radio committee was appointed, as I recall it within a certain length of time, but I was told by some hon. member opposite -I think I am right in saying that it was my hon. friend the leader of the opposition among others who told me-that there were certain gentlemen on his side of the house who wished to debate this matter and that he hoped I would not take it up before the Easter recess.

speechtext: I know the Prime Minister would not want to put words in my mouth. I cannot recall having said that and I am quite sure that I did not. It may have been someone else who made mention of that, but so far as I am concerned any intimation with respect to hon. members having something to say applied as much to the radio broadcasting committee as it did to this one.

We were drawing rapidly to the moment of adjournment at Easter, and I repeated a previous suggestion that it should not take any time at all to set up the committee and that if hon. members wished to discuss matters relevant thereto later on, it could be done on a report of the committee or when the committee was making its report. But I know-I am not sufficiently clear in my mind to say positively that it was from the leader of the opposition'-I certainly received an intimation from some hon. gentleman opposite in the clearest manner possible that there were hon. members on the other side who wished to speak on this motion and that the debate would take a considerable time. It was that reason and that reason alone which prevented me from bringing forward this motion before the Easter recess. As I say, it was the duty of the leader of the
opposition, if he regarded the setting up of this committee as of national importance, to have risen- in his seat and asked me as leader of the government to see that the motion was placed before the house before the session got along too far.

Mr. GRAYDON I do not know where my right hon. friend got that idea. It may have been, as he says, that someone intimated that some hon. members wished to speak, but I never knew that there was going to be a long debate. There has not been a long debate at this stage.

If that was in the back
of my right hon. friend's mind why did he

I think the
order of committees was established by the way requested names for memberships were received from the different parties in the house. I cannot tell the house why, but there was special difficulty in certain quarters opposite in obtaining the names of members for the war expenditures committee. The desire of the government was to get all these committees set up as rapidly as possible. As I said this afternoon, the committees for the most part were set up at an earlier date this year than has been the case for many years past in this parliament. I come back to the position that if the committee was not set up earlier the leader of the opposition is responsible more than anyone else for not having asked the government that it should be set up at an earlier time. I repeat the challenge I have made, to look at the records of Hansard to see whether my hon. friend at any time asked that this committee because of its importance should be appointed without further delay.
In regard to the points that have been raised in the course of the debate this afternoon I should like to say this. With the exception of the changing of a word or two, the reasons for which I mentioned when the matter was being discussed before, the resolution before the house to-day is in the identical terms of the resolution which has been passed by the House of Commons at Westminster every year since this war began, and which was adopted in the first instance in the third year of the last war. The British parliament has had experience in dealing with public expenditures unequalled by any other free parliament in the world. The war expenditures at Westminster are colossal compared with the war expenditures made by this parliament. I personally have felt that the reasons which have governed the powers and procedure of the committee at Westminster must be very strong indeed, or the government at Westminster would never have consented to having the powers given, limited in some respects as they are, and the particular procedure adopted which exists in respect to the war expenditures committee of the United Kingdom. Everything that has been done with regard to the war expenditures committee at Westminster has been done for the best and soundest of reasons. I make that statement the more emphatically because there are many hon. gentlemen opposite me who, when Sir John Wardlaw Milne was here, who is chairman of the war

expenditures committee and a leading Conservative in the British parliament, had conversations with him on this very matter. They asked about the procedure in the British house and the powers of its war expenditures committee and received from him direct the reasons which governed at Westminster in having, not some sessions of the war expenditures committee held in camera, but all its sessions. There have been no sessions of the war expenditures committee in Great Britain held in public. The British parliament, which is most zealous in its supervision of expenditures and is the custodian of the interests of the people of the United Kingdom, has not reached that decision without the very best of reasons, and I am convinced that they are the very soundest reasons in time of war.
There is one thing I have tried to do in the discharge of my responsibility here, and that is to have nothing done in this parliament which was merely to embarrass the British parliament or the British war effort or the war effort of the United States or that of any of our allies or our own war effort. I have had to ask myself time and again: Will I remain misunderstood in regard to a particular attitude I am taking because I do not come out and say something that would' be very popular and meet with general acclaim, or shall I remain silent, and follow the procedure that I know to be wisest, though it may not be generally understood to the degree one would wish among the people?
This is a case in point. I should like to see all these inquiries made in the open. I am just as anxious to have publicity on these matters as anybody could be, more anxious indeed than any other member in the house, because I have more to lose than an}' other man if scandals should develop in our war effort; or anything improper take place as a result of inadequate supervision on the part of the government. I want to see this war expenditures committee carry on its duties. I want to see it go into all matters of war expenditure just as fully as it possibly can. I want to see the opposition join with members of the government in seeing that the investigations of that committee are made just as thorough as they can possibly be made. But I do not want to make a departure here which is going possibly to result in something happening in Canada whic-h is the very thing which the British parliament has sought to avoid having happen as a result of investigations in time of war. I take my stand on the experience and wisdom of the parlia-

ment at Westminster in dealing with expenditures in time of war, and I am prepared to say to this house and to the country: any right, any privilege, any opportunity that is given to the committee on war expenditures at Westminster I would like our committee to have and I will support in this house. Surely that is going as far as any committee could wish to go. I am ready to have any power given to this committee or to any of its subcommittees that is given to the war expenditures committee in the United Kingdom. I not only would be willing to give it to our committee but I wish them to have it.
I could go at some length into the reasons why meetings are held in camera and as to the other points raised, but in a previous debate I discussed, I think, every one of them and I do not wish to detain the house by a discussion at length this afternoon.

The composition of this House of Commons is determined by the country, and the composition of committees of this house is based upon the composition of its membership.

The procedure covered by the proposed amendment is based pretty much upon the English practice. The proviso to the present section 56 definitely limits the power of an insurance officer to disallow a claim for benefit or to disqualify a claimant.. This results in a rather cumbersome and slow procedure, and the amendment proposed is designed to give the commission power by regulation to extend the power of the insurance officer to disallow and disqualify. This disallowance or disqualification by the insurance officer will be subject to the provisions of section 57 of the act, which gives the claimant the right of appeal to a court of referees. The amendment does not therefore cut down the right of the claimant but should expedite the adjudication of his claim. If the circumstances so require, the insurance officer may disallow the claim or disqualify the claimant, notifying him at once as to his right of appeal. There are many cases where it is amply evident to the insurance officer that the claimant is not qualified, as for example where his state of health makes it evident that he is not capable of taking employment. Under the present provisions the insurance officer may not disqualify a claimant under such circumstances, though it may be perfectly plain that the claim will without doubt be disallowed by the court of referees.
The suggested amendment would assist the claimant in knowing at the earliest date possible, and not fooling him, as sometimes happens, what disposition is to be made of his claim, and if he wishes he may appeal that decision to the court of referees. The situation now is that an applicant because the officer has no power to deal with the matter, may be led

and I think it may be fairly stated that those who gave evidence before that committee were about as good a cross-section of organized employers and employees as one could find in the dominion-it was agreed by the com-

mittee that the ceiling should be raised from $2,000 to $2,400. This, of course, covers only what one might call the white-collar class. There is no ceiling on the weekly-paid employees and piece-paid employees. While at some later date it may be necessary to raise the ceiling to $3,000, my hon. friend can rest assured that if a recommendation in those terms should come from the committee, it would certainly receive the favourable consideration of the government.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS TO EMPLOYEES IN RECEIPT OF UP TO $2,400 A YEAR
speechtext: That is the point. The ceiling for labour is not $2,400. It is for what the minister calls the white-collar class. Why should there be that difference?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS TO EMPLOYEES IN RECEIPT OF UP TO $2,400 A YEAR
speechtext: That is easily explained. Under war conditions, with overtime and cost of living bonus, the original calculations have been more or less thrown out of balance, and unless an amendment of this kind is made it is fair to assume that there will be thousands of workers who, when the act was originally passed, were under its jurisdiction, who would be forced out of its provisions. An amendment of this kind is therefore necessary. It may be in the course of the next year we may have to fall in line with the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver East. We cannot tell. But I think that it is absolutely necessary, that it is in the best interests of the working people themselves and also that it is good government policy that as many as possible should be brought within the jurisdiction of this legislation. Where we have what might be described as a wage structure on the upgrade, every effort should be made not only to maintain but possibly to increase the coverage, so that when war is concluded there will be at least one cushion to take care of any possible dislocation which may take place in the industrial or commercial set-up of our country.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS TO EMPLOYEES IN RECEIPT OF UP TO $2,400 A YEAR

I quite agree, but I have two men working in my plant, one holding a clerical position and the other running a machine. The man who runs the machine at an hourly rate does not come under any ceiling. The man who works in the clerical position has a ceiling of $2,400. I do not see why there should be that difference. They should all come under it, and the coverage should be on all employees. Then, as the minister has said, that coverage should be as large as possible.

Unemployment Insurance Act

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS TO EMPLOYEES IN RECEIPT OF UP TO $2,400 A YEAR
speechtext: This was the most contentious point which came before the committee. After considerable discussion among the parties this was the figure agreed upon. When the workers and employers are in agreement, as they were in this instance, I am always loath to go counter to their advice. If my memory serves me correctly, I received representations stating that the maximum should be $4,800 a year, and I am inclined to agree with that. I do not know why I should not be included within the provisions of the act, or why all other hon. members should not -looking forward to the next general election. But, be that as it may, I followed out what I thought was sound advice given to me by this committee, after mature consideration of all the factors involved in the briefs submitted by employee and employer organizations.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS TO EMPLOYEES IN RECEIPT OF UP TO $2,400 A YEAR
speechtext: There is only one good reason I can see why a clerk, for instance, should have a ceiling, namely, that perhaps he has better continuity of employment than the man in the workshop. But there are many people in Canada .employed in big organizations, such as banks, who never want to come under it at all. They are what might be described as white-collar men, and they are getting clear. It seems to me that this is leaving out a class. People who say they have no hazards do not want to come in at all. One pays insurance, and hopes he will never benefit from it. That is the state of mind in which insurance is paid. If interests are to be pooled, then people who do not have hazards should be pooled with those who do have hazards, because the people who have the hazards are necessary to the community. I cannot understand this difference, and I do not think it should be there.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: I recall that in the railway committee it was stated that some twelve or thirteen million dollars was set aside for deferred maintenance, an item which would not be allowed to any private company but which was set up by the Canadian National because it made no difference to their statement, inasmuch as they were not subject to taxation. What would become of that money, and why would it not be available to the company to finance these capital expenditures, instead of asking the government for authority to issue $6,000,000 odd in securities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
The deferred maintenance reserve is for deferred maintenance rather

than for capital additions and betterments. I may add that the $17,000,000 is available from reserves for depreciation and debt discount amortization, but nothing is taken from the deferred maintenance reserve, because the purpose of this expenditure is not maintenance.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: I appreciate that the purpose is capital, but inasmuch as the railway company must lean on the government for all of its capital expenditures, nevertheless there is this amount for deferred maintenance which is an extraordinary amount and one not allowed to private companies. I am suggesting that unless it is absolutely necessary for its working capital account-and I do not think that it is because it has ample working capital-it is hard to understand why this money is being made available to the railway company for its capital expenditure instead of borrowing more through the government authorization.
